result.summary: The chapter tells the story of Oeneus of Calydon and his family: the birth of Meleager, the Calydonian boar hunt, and Meleager's death when the brand is burnt. It then follows Oeneus's later marriage, his son Tydeus, and his downfall at the hands of Agrius's sons until Diomedes avenges him.

scenes.title: Oeneus and his children
scenes.summary: Oeneus receives the vine from Dionysus, marries Althaea and has many children, including Deianira, for whom Hercules wrestles Achelous.

scenes.title: The brand and the boar
scenes.summary: The Fates foretell Meleager's death with the brand, which Althaea hides. Oeneus neglects Artemis, who sends a ravaging boar.
scenes.stakes: Meleager's life is tied to the brand; Calydon's land and people are threatened by the boar.

scenes.title: The Calydonian boar hunt
scenes.summary: Heroes gather and hunt the boar with Atalanta. Meleager kills it and gives the skin to Atalanta, and Thestius's sons take it from her.
scenes.stakes: The hunters risk death from the boar, and Atalanta's honor is at stake.

scenes.title: Death of Meleager
scenes.summary: Meleager kills Thestius's sons; Althaea burns the brand and he dies. An alternate version has a war with the Curetes. Althaea and Cleopatra hang themselves.
scenes.stakes: Meleager's life, and Althaea's divided loyalty between son and brothers.

scenes.title: Periboea and Tydeus
scenes.summary: Oeneus marries Periboea, with varying accounts of her origin and of Tydeus's parentage. Tydeus is exiled, marries Deipyle, fathers Diomedes and dies at Thebes.
scenes.stakes: Periboea's life and Tydeus's safety in exile.

scenes.title: Fall and avenging of Oeneus
scenes.summary: Agrius's sons seize the kingdom and torment Oeneus. Diomedes kills most of them and restores order, but the survivors kill Oeneus in Arcadia, and Diomedes buries him at Oenoe.
scenes.stakes: Oeneus's kingdom and life are lost to Agrius's sons.

notable_quotes.reason: The Fates' prophecy tying Meleager's life to a burning brand.

analysis.text: Neglecting a god's honor brings disaster, as Oeneus forgetting Artemis leads to the boar and ultimately his family's ruin.
Apollodorus gathers competing versions from Hesiod, Pisander and others, showing the Library's role as a compendium of myth traditions.

legacy.text: The Calydonian boar hunt and Meleager's brand became favorite subjects in Greek and Roman art and in later poetry, such as Swinburne's Atalanta in Calydon (1865).

fun_facts.text: Apollodorus cites several lost epics here, such as the Thebaid and the Alcmaeonis, which survive only through such references.

language_notes.text: "Leaped over the ditch" refers to a trench Oeneus was digging or had dug around his land; leaping it was treated as a deadly insult.
"Begotten on Althaea by Dionysus" means Dionysus, not Oeneus, was said to be Deianira's real father.
Hercules' wrestling match with the river-god Achelous for Deianira's hand is a well-known contest; Hercules won and married her.
"Brand" means a piece of burning wood; here the log's life is tied to Meleager's life.
"First fruits" are the earliest produce of the harvest, offered to the gods before the rest was used.
"Undesignedly" means by accident, without intending it.
"Thinking scorn" means thinking it shameful; "in the face of men" means in spite of the men present.
The brand is a log of wood that the Fates said would fix Meleager's lifespan; Althaea had kept it. Burning it ends his life.
Curetes: a people of Aetolia, here at war with the Calydonians over the boar's skin.
The Thebaid and Hesiod's poems are lost or fragmentary epics; Apollodorus cites them to show differing versions of the myth.
Zeus is named here by this translation's source; the claim is that Oeneus's incest with Gorge was divinely willed, making Tydeus her son and brother-like.
"To wit" is archaic for "that is to say" and introduces the list of names.
"Betimes" means in good time, early; the two sons fled before Diomedes arrived.

context_notes.text: Calydon was a city in Aetolia, in western Greece. Dionysus was the god of wine, so the gift of the vine is fitting.
The Fates were the goddesses who spun and fixed each person's destiny, including the length of life.
Artemis, goddess of hunting and wild places, was quick to punish those who slighted her.
The long list gathers famous heroes, including Jason, Theseus, and the Dioscuri Castor and Pollux, from across Greece.
The expedition of the Seven against Thebes was Adrastus's campaign to put Polynices on the Theban throne; Tydeus was one of the seven champions.
A hearth was a sacred place of refuge, so killing a man there was a serious violation of religious custom.

literary_notes.text: The Fates' prophecy tying Meleager's life to the brand anticipates his death later in the story.
The hidden brand stands for Meleager's life, and Althaea's act of protecting it shows a mother's care.
Artemis is shown as vengeful, answering a single omitted offering with disproportionate destruction.
The woman is first to wound the boar, yet the men soon try to deny her the prize.
The compiler offers a rival version with "some say," showing the mythographer's habit of recording variants rather than choosing one.
The mourning women are turned into birds, a common mythic way of fixing grief into the natural world.
The long list of Agrius's sons stresses the size of the faction that overwhelms Oeneus, in epic list style.
